text: Are the stereotypes about women true? Number four, women are naturally competitive with each other. Wrong. Research confirms that competition between women is strongest in environments where leadership roles are scarce, meaning the system creates our rivalry, not our nature. More research found that women outperform men in collaboration and creativity in small group settings. We are naturally wired to build community. The catty women narrative is what happens when you give limited seats to tell everyone to fight for one, but when there's enough room at the table, we collaborate. That competition is manufactured. So let me get it straight. She claims that competition between women is not natural, but created by the system. No, this is where I would disagree right away. Competition is not something that is manufactured. It is natural, not just for women, but for everyone. Men compete with men. Women compete with women. Everyone competes with everyone. That is how humans behave in general. If you want access to better resources, better partners, better positions, you have to compete. That is basic evolutionary logic. Survival and selection always involve some form of competition. So the idea that competition between women is not natural at all, but only created by the system, that is simply not correct. Now, with that said, I think she is partially right about one thing. The environment does matter. When resources are scarce, positions, attention, opportunities, competition increases. That applies to men and women alike. So yes, the system can amplify rivalry, but it doesn't create it from nothing. Now to her second point, that women outperform men in collaboration and creativity in small groups. Here again, there is a kernel of truth, but we need to be precise. If you look at personality research, one of the most consistent findings is that women, on average, score higher in agreeableness. This has been shown across many studies and cultures. For example, a meta-analysis, Gender Differences in Personality, by Feingold, published in Psychological Bulletin, as well as cross-cultural research by Costa and McRae, and more recent, large-scale studies like Weisberg et al. Agreeableness is strongly linked to cooperative behavior. So if you put people in environments where collaboration, communication, and coordination matter, especially in smaller, less hierarchical groups, those traits can be an advantage. That is likely what these studies are picking up. But again, that doesn't mean women are better at collaboration in some universal sense. It means that different traits perform better in different environments. Because if you move into more competitive, hierarchical, or high-pressure settings, traits that are more common in men, on average, like assertiveness, risk-taking, or dominance, can also become advantageous. So once again, the reality is more nuanced. Yes, women, on average, tend to be more agreeable, which can support cooperation in certain settings. Yes, environment can increase or decrease competition. But saying that competition is manufactured and that women are naturally non-competitive, that is simply not accurate.
